analysis.one_liner: Raises the contract size threshold for prevailing-wage rules on federal construction while strengthening penalties for wage violations.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 22 House Democrats, was referred to a House subcommittee in March 1995 and never received a vote or hearing before that Congress ended in January 1997.
analysis.plain_summary: The Davis-Bacon Act requires federal construction contractors to pay workers the prevailing local wage. This bill would have lifted the contract size at which that rule applies — exempting new construction under $100,000 and repair jobs under $15,000 — while adding new worker protections on covered jobs, including double damages for willful underpayment, attorney's fees, faster complaint procedures, and a rule treating several small contracts on the same project as one so contractors cannot split jobs to dodge the law.
analysis.who_benefits: If passed, construction workers on larger federal jobs would gain stronger enforcement: twice the unpaid wages for willful violations, attorney's fees, a right to administrative complaints with deadlines, and pay suspension for contractors who file late payroll reports [S3]. Small contractors doing sub-threshold federal work would be freed from the prevailing-wage paperwork and rates [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Covered construction workers and small contractors

how_it_helps.text: Employers who willfully fail to pay required wages would owe affected workers twice the unpaid amount, plus attorney's fees and court costs, and workers could sue in federal or state court [S3].

Two or more contracts on the same project that individually fall under the threshold but together exceed it would be treated as one contract, with any interested person able to sue the contracting agency and recover prevailing wages plus interest and fees [S3].

Workers could file administrative complaints that the Labor Department must resolve within 120 days, could seek judicial review of coverage decisions, and agencies would have to suspend payments to contractors who fail to submit certified payroll reports on time [S3].
The bill would leave stricter state, local, and tribal wage rules in place on federally financed contracts, letting the toughest applicable standard govern [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Construction workers on small federal contracts would lose prevailing-wage protection, since jobs under $100,000 (new construction) or $15,000 (alteration and repair) would be exempt [S2][S3]. Covered contractors would face tougher enforcement, double damages, debarment for up to three years for repeat violators, and contract termination for underpaying workers [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Workers on small federal jobs; contractors on covered ones

drawbacks.text: Exempting smaller contracts would remove the prevailing-wage floor from many repair and alteration jobs, letting those workers be paid whatever the local market on non-federal jobs happens to be [S2][S3].

Prevailing wage determinations would have to consider wages on all projects regardless of funding source, which in heavily unionized areas could pull federal wage rates down toward lower non-union levels [S3].

Allowing below-prevailing pay for registered apprentices, trainees, and helpers — while a standard way to encourage training — would let employers pay some workers less than the full rate on covered jobs [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: This was a genuine trade. Workers who stayed covered would get materially stronger tools to collect what they were owed, and the anti-contract-splitting rule would close a common loophole. But the price was pulling a large share of smaller federal jobs out from under the wage floor entirely, and the new wage-survey standard risked lowering rates in high-union markets. Whether workers as a whole came out ahead depended on how many jobs fell under the new thresholds — a number the bill text does not provide.

outcome.mechanism: It went to the House Economic and Educational Opportunities Committee on the day it was introduced, was sent down to its Workforce Protections subcommittee three weeks later, and sat there until the Congress ended in January 1997 — no hearing, no vote, no floor action.

narrative.text: Rep. William Clay of Missouri introduced the bill on February 15, 1995, joined by 14 original cosponsors, and it was referred to the Committee on Economic and Educational Opportunities [S1][S3].
On March 10, 1995, the bill was referred to the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections, and no further action was recorded for the remainder of the 104th Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Workers on smaller federal construction jobs came out ahead: the prevailing-wage floor the bill would have lifted at their level stayed in place. Nothing was gained, though, on the enforcement side, which died with the bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Workers on small federal jobs kept coverage

sides.party_line_note: All 22 cosponsors were Democrats, and the bill died in a committee then controlled by Republicans without a hearing or vote [S4][S5].

industries.note: Small contractors under the new thresholds would be freed from prevailing-wage rates, but covered contractors would face double damages, debarment for three to five years, payment suspensions for late payroll reports, and contract termination for underpaying workers. The industry's interest in the threshold relief runs against the wage floor that benefits workers.

Unions generally benefit from prevailing-wage enforcement and the anti-contract-splitting rule, and the bill allowed wage-determination data from all projects, which could dilute the union-heavy rates current determinations often reflect. Net effect depends on the coverage shift.
